title: Concurrency: collections, coordination and deadlocks
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic JEE-style quizzes for the backend and AI-engineering interview roadmap: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code writing, plus multi-correct questions. Language core, concurrency, DSA, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, LLM and agent engineering.
description: ConcurrentHashMap, BlockingQueue, CopyOnWriteArrayList, asyncio.Queue, latches, barriers, semaphores, the four deadlock conditions, lock ordering and reading thread dumps.
source: Oracle Java docs (java.util.concurrent); Java Concurrency in Practice; Python queue, threading and asyncio docs; py-spy README; Baeldung; GeeksforGeeks

options.text: get then put is a check-then-act sequence, so two threads can read the same n and lose an increment.
options.why: Correct: each call is thread-safe but the pair is not atomic; use hits.merge(key, 1, Integer::sum).

options.text: ConcurrentHashMap.put throws ConcurrentModificationException whenever two writers collide on one bucket.
options.why: The map never throws it; its iterators are weakly consistent.

options.text: Autoboxing of n + 1 creates a shared Integer cache entry that two threads corrupt.
options.why: Boxing a local value is harmless; the race is on the shared map entry.

options.text: get() may block until another thread finishes its put(), so threads queue up behind each other.
options.why: Reads in ConcurrentHashMap are non-blocking.

questions.explanation: Use merge, compute or computeIfAbsent (atomic per key) or a LongAdder as the value. Same bug shape: containsKey then put.

questions.prompt: Seven threads each call await() once on the same new CyclicBarrier(3). How many of them are still blocked after everything that can happen has happened?
questions.explanation: The barrier trips for every group of 3: two groups (6 threads) pass, and the seventh waits for two partners that never arrive (verified by running it). The barrier is reusable, which a CountDownLatch is not.

questions.prompt: A Semaphore is created with new Semaphore(2). A thread calls acquire() once, then release() twice. What does availablePermits() return afterwards?
questions.explanation: Start 2, acquire leaves 1, two releases give 3. A semaphore does not remember who acquired; release() can raise the count above the initial value (verified by running it). That is why you release in finally and only after a successful acquire.

questions.prompt: ConcurrentHashMap, unlike HashMap, rejects null keys and null values.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: put("a", null) throws NullPointerException, because a null from get() would be ambiguous between absent and mapped to null.

options.text: False
options.why: HashMap allows one null key and null values, but ConcurrentHashMap throws NullPointerException for both.

questions.explanation: This design avoids ambiguity in concurrent code, where you cannot do containsKey after get atomically.

questions.prompt: Match each concurrent collection with the situation it fits best.

right.text: High-throughput shared map with per-key atomic updates
Rarely changed list of listeners that is iterated constantly
Bounded hand-off that blocks producers when full
Unbounded lock-free queue where take() never blocks
Consumers must always take the highest priority item first

questions.explanation: Note that ConcurrentLinkedQueue has no blocking take(); wrap it or use LinkedBlockingQueue when consumers must wait. The synchronized wrapper is the coarse-lock distractor.

options.text: It prints [1, 2, 3, 99] and the loop never sees 99.
options.why: Correct: the iterator works on a snapshot taken when the loop began, so there is no exception and no 99 in the loop.

options.text: It throws ConcurrentModificationException on the next iteration.
options.why: That is the ArrayList behaviour (verified); COW iterators never throw it.

options.text: It prints [1, 2, 3] because the add is ignored during iteration.
options.why: The add succeeds on a fresh copy of the array; only the running iterator is unaffected.

options.text: It loops forever as 99 keeps being appended.
options.why: The snapshot has three elements, so the loop ends after 3 steps.

questions.explanation: Each mutation copies the whole array: great for read-mostly data, terrible for write-heavy lists.

questions.prompt: Complete the sentences about java.util.concurrent synchronizers.
questions.text: A {1} blocks waiters until its count reaches zero and cannot be reset. A {2} makes a fixed number of threads wait for each other and is reusable. A {3} limits how many threads hold permits at once.
questions.explanation: Phaser is a reusable barrier with a dynamic number of parties, and Exchanger swaps objects between two threads.

questions.prompt: Write Java that starts 3 worker threads (each runs doWork()) and makes the main thread wait until all 3 have finished. Use a CountDownLatch and make sure the count goes down even if doWork() throws.

checks.label: calls countDown in a finally block

questions.explanation: Without finally, one failing worker leaves the latch above zero and main waits forever. Executors or a loop over a list are equally valid; await(timeout, unit) is a safer variant.

questions.prompt: Write an async Python function limited(sem, url) that waits for an asyncio.Semaphore before awaiting fetch(url) and returns the result, so at most N fetches run at once.

checks.label: uses the semaphore (async with or acquire)

questions.explanation: async with releases the permit even if fetch raises. In threads the same idea uses threading.Semaphore with a plain with statement.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: Iterating over Collections.synchronizedMap(map).entrySet() still needs a manual synchronized(map) block.
questions.reason: ConcurrentHashMap iterators are weakly consistent and never throw ConcurrentModificationException.

whys.a: R is a true statement, but it does not explain why the synchronized wrapper needs manual locking.
whys.b: Correct: both true. The wrapper locks each method call, not the whole iteration; R describes a different class and does not explain A.
whys.c: R is true, so option c (R false) is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so option d (A false) is wrong.

questions.explanation: Compound actions on a synchronized wrapper (iteration, check-then-act) need the client to hold the wrapper's lock.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: A worker thread may call asyncio.Queue.put_nowait() directly to hand items to coroutines.
questions.reason: asyncio.Queue is designed for coroutines on a single event loop and is documented as not thread-safe.

whys.a: A is false, so the pair cannot be a valid explanation.
whys.b: A is false, so option b is wrong.
whys.c: A is false, so option c (A true) is wrong.
whys.d: Correct: R is true and A is false. From another thread use loop.call_soon_threadsafe(q.put_nowait, item) or asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe.

questions.explanation: queue.Queue is for threads, asyncio.Queue for coroutines. Bridging needs call_soon_threadsafe.

questions.prompt:
A jstack dump shows a thread with:

"worker-1" java.lang.Thread.State: BLOCKED (on object monitor)
    at Inventory.reserve(Inventory.java:42)
    - waiting to lock <0x000000076ab62208> (a java.lang.Object)

What does it mean?

options.text: It is trying to enter a synchronized block held by another thread.
options.why: Correct: BLOCKED means waiting to acquire a monitor; search the dump for "locked <0x000000076ab62208>" to find the holder.

options.text: It called Object.wait() and is now waiting for another thread to call notify().
options.why: That shows as WAITING (on object monitor) with a "waiting on" line.

options.text: It is parked on a ReentrantLock, a Condition or a BlockingQueue.
options.why: That shows as WAITING (parking), with "parking to wait for".

options.text: It is sleeping inside Thread.sleep() and will wake up by itself.
options.why: That is TIMED_WAITING (sleeping).

questions.explanation: BLOCKED vs WAITING is the thread-dump interview question. For deadlocks, jstack prints a "Found one Java-level deadlock" section. Also: jcmd <pid> Thread.print and kill -3.

questions.prompt: Select all conditions that must hold simultaneously for a deadlock to occur (the Coffman conditions).

options.text: Mutual exclusion
options.why: Correct: at least one resource can be held by only one thread at a time.

options.text: Hold and wait
options.why: Correct: a thread holds one resource while waiting for another.

options.text: No preemption
options.why: Correct: resources cannot be forcibly taken from a holder.

options.text: Circular wait
options.why: Correct: a cycle of threads each waits for a resource held by the next.

options.text: Thread starvation
options.why: Not required: starvation is about unfairness, not a cycle.

options.text: Priority inversion
options.why: Not required: it is a scheduling problem, not a deadlock condition.

questions.explanation: Break any one condition: lock ordering removes circular wait, tryLock with timeout removes hold-and-wait, and so on. The answer to 'how many conditions' is 4.

questions.prompt: Class Account has an int field id and an int field balance. Write transfer(Account from, Account to, int amt) so that two opposite transfers (A to B and B to A) can never deadlock, by always locking the account with the smaller id first.

checks.label: orders the two accounts by id

questions.explanation: A global lock order removes circular wait. If ids can tie, break ties with a separate tie-lock or identityHashCode. Verified to finish with 2 opposite-direction threads. ReentrantLock.tryLock with back-off is the alternative.

questions.prompt: A Python worker process hangs in production and you must see what each thread is doing without restarting or modifying it. Which command does that?

options.text: py-spy dump --pid <pid>
options.why: Correct: py-spy samples the process from outside and prints each thread's current Python stack.

options.text: jstack <pid>
options.why: jstack inspects JVM processes only.

options.text: kill -9 <pid>
options.why: SIGKILL ends the process and destroys the evidence.

options.text: python -m pdb <pid>
options.why: pdb launches scripts; it cannot attach to a running process by pid.

questions.explanation: py-spy needs ptrace permission (often sudo, or CAP_SYS_PTRACE in containers). Alternatives: faulthandler.dump_traceback registered on a signal, or --native for C frames.
